[Thinking]
**Expanding narrative structure**

I need to expand a story into five sections. I can't just copy everything verbatim, but I can base it on the original material. So, I'm thinking about creating a narrative similar to a news feature, which would include elements like background, escalation, and responses. Maybe I should also involve expert opinions and discuss implications. Let's get started on this approach and see how it all comes together!
[/Thinking]

Section 1  
Jeremy Hunt, the health secretary, found himself locked in an increasingly surreal social media confrontation with comedy actor Ralf Little after a clash over the state of mental health services in the NHS spilled onto Twitter. The dispute was sparked by Hunt’s appearance on The Andrew Marr Show, where he claimed that under his watch the health service had delivered “the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe”. Within hours, Little – long familiar to TV audiences for his role as put‑upon son Anthony in The Royle Family – accused Hunt of “knowingly lying” to the public, challenging the minister to sue him if his statement was untrue. What might have been dismissed as a celebrity outburst instead evolved into a days‑long, highly publicised fact‑checking battle.

Section 2  
Little’s allegation touched a nerve. Hunt had only recently been forced to correct the parliamentary record after confidently asserting that there were 30,000 more mental health workers than before – a figure later shown to be inflated by a factor of more than forty. Stung by the renewed accusation, Hunt did not ignore the actor; instead, he replied a week later with a detailed Twitter thread filled with statistics, charts and comparisons. He insisted that improvements in access, investment and workforce numbers justified his original claim, and he goaded Little to respond in kind, “double daring” him to demonstrate that the figures were wrong. The unusually combative tone from a cabinet minister quickly drew attention from political commentators and health campaigners alike.

Section 3  
Little accepted the challenge with enthusiasm. Over the next day he compiled and posted a sprawling, meticulously sourced thread of more than 40 tweets, attempting to dismantle Hunt’s narrative point by point. Citing data from NHS England, parliamentary briefings and the independent fact‑checking organisation Full Fact, he argued that funding pledges had not translated into frontline capacity, that many services were still turning people away, and that staff shortages remained severe despite headline promises. The thread was shared tens of thousands of times, pushing the argument beyond the usual Westminster bubble and into the timelines of ordinary NHS staff, patients and comedians who began weighing in with their own experiences of accessing mental health care.

Section 4  
Refusing to let the matter rest, Hunt returned to Twitter on the following Monday with another lengthy thread, this time stretching to 26 tweets. In it he attempted to clarify his position, though the sequence became muddled, with tweets appearing out of order and references looping back on themselves. Hunt reiterated that there were thousands of mental health nurses currently in training and pointed to a 25% increase in nurse training places announced for that September. He also leaned on international validation, quoting from a New York Times article that had praised aspects of the NHS’s mental health reforms – though that piece, critics noted, had already been corrected multiple times after Labour’s former shadow minister for mental health, Luciana Berger, disputed several of its claims.

Section 5  
What began as a spat between a cabinet minister and a sitcom star grew into a wider argument about political honesty and the gap between official statistics and lived reality. Mental health professionals weighed in to say that while there had been welcome policy commitments and some local innovations, everyday access to care still fell far short of demand, particularly for children and adolescents. For campaigners, the row underlined how easily numbers could be marshalled to tell conflicting stories, depending on what was counted and over what timeframe. For many observers, the most striking aspect of the episode was not that a comedian had challenged a senior politician, but that it took a public Twitter feud to force such a detailed, line‑by‑line examination of the government’s record on mental health.
